title: Psalm 96: A New Song for All the Earth
summary: The psalm calls the whole earth to sing a new song to the LORD and to tell the nations of his glory, because every other god is an idol and the LORD made the heavens. The families of the nations are invited to bring offerings into his courts and worship him. Finally the sea, the fields, and the trees of the forest are called to rejoice, because the LORD is coming to judge the world in righteousness.
story: Psalm 96 is one of the kingship psalms of Book IV (Psalms 93 and 95 to 99), which answer the fall of David's house mourned in Psalm 89 by declaring that the LORD himself still reigns. Psalm 95 called Israel to worship and warned them against hardened hearts. Psalm 96 opens the doors much wider: the invitation now goes to “all the earth”, to the nations and their families, and even to the sea and the trees. The movement is from Israel's worship to the world's. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3) is heard here as a song the nations themselves are asked to sing.
historical:
The psalm has no heading in Hebrew. Almost all of it appears again in 1 Chronicles 16:23-33, as part of the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant (the gold-covered chest that stood for God's throne among his people) into Jerusalem. Scholars debate which came first: some think the Chronicler, writing after the exile, stitched together existing psalms (96, 105, and 106) for the occasion; others think the psalm was drawn from an older celebration. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, gives the psalm a heading linking it both to David and to the rebuilding of the house after the captivity, which shows how later Jewish readers heard it: as a song for a restored temple after the exile.

Many phrases also resemble the second half of Isaiah (chapters 40 to 55), which speaks of a new song, of idols as nothing, and of good news announced to the nations. Some scholars therefore date the psalm to the exile or after it; others think Isaiah and the psalm both drew on older temple worship. The kingship psalms were probably sung at the great festivals in Jerusalem, though the details of that setting are debated.
cultural:
In the ancient world each nation had its gods, and conquering peoples often carried off the statues of defeated nations' gods as trophies. To tell the nations that “all the gods of the nations are idols” (verse 5) was therefore a bold claim, and the Hebrew makes it with a pun: the gods, elohim, are only elilim, worthless things. The LORD, by contrast, made the heavens that those gods were supposed to rule.

The call to “bring an offering and enter His courts” (verse 8) would have startled an Israelite, because the temple courts were carefully bounded and foreigners had limited access. The word for offering, minchah, was also used for tribute paid by a subject nation to its overlord. The picture is of the nations coming to the great King's palace with gifts, not as defeated enemies but as worshipers. “The LORD reigns” (verse 10) was a coronation cry, the kind of shout raised when a new king took the throne (compare 2 Kings 9:13).
literary: The psalm is built in widening circles. Verses 1 to 6 call Israel (and all the earth) to sing and give the reason: the LORD is great and the gods are nothing. Verses 7 to 9 echo the pattern of Psalm 29, with its threefold “Ascribe to the LORD”, but where Psalm 29 addressed heavenly beings, this psalm addresses the families of the nations. Verse 10 gives the message to be announced. Verses 11 to 13 widen the circle to heaven, earth, sea, field, and forest. The repeated commands (sing three times, ascribe three times) create momentum, and the psalm ends by doubling its last reason: “for He is coming”, and then again, “He is coming to judge the earth”.

outline.t: Sing a new song and tell the nations
The LORD made the heavens; the gods are idols
The families of the nations are called to worship
The message: the LORD reigns and will judge
Creation rejoices before the coming Judge

doctrines.note: Israel's praise is meant to be overheard. The psalm commands God's people to declare his glory among the nations and invites those nations to come and worship. The concern for the whole world is not a New Testament addition; it is sung here.
The gods of the nations are “idols”, empty things, because only the LORD made the heavens. The psalm refuses to treat worship as a matter of local preference.

God's coming to judge is presented as good news that makes even the trees sing. Judgment here means setting the world right with righteousness and faithfulness, which is what an oppressed and disordered world longs for.

words.note: Basar, to bring news, usually good news. Translated “proclaim” in verse 2. The Greek translation uses the verb from which the New Testament's word for gospel comes, and Isaiah 40:9 and 52:7 use the same Hebrew verb for the herald announcing that God reigns. The psalm and Isaiah share a single idea: the good news is that the LORD is King.

Elil, a worthless thing, a nothing. The word sounds like elohim (gods) and seems chosen for that reason. It is a verdict, not a description: whatever the nations honor, it cannot make or rule the heavens.
Chadash, new. A “new song” in the Psalms is usually a response to a fresh act of God's rescue (Psalms 33, 40, 98, 144, 149). Here the newness also lies in who sings it: the whole earth.

Shaphat, to judge. In Hebrew the word covers both passing sentence and ruling, rescuing, and setting things right, which is why the judges of Israel were also its deliverers. When God comes to judge the earth, the psalm expects a world put back in order.

christ: The New Testament announces as fact what this psalm calls for. The gospel (the “good news” of verse 2's verb) goes out to the nations, and Paul tells the Athenians that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man he has appointed, raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31), language that echoes the last line of this psalm. The coming of the LORD to judge becomes, for Christians, the return of Christ. Some early Christian writers, Justin Martyr among them in the second century, knew a form of verse 10 that read that the LORD reigns from the tree, and they read it of the cross; that wording is not in the Hebrew or in the main Greek manuscripts, but it shows how early the church heard its King in this song.
questions: The psalm expects the nations to hear about God from the worship of his people. What would outsiders learn about God by overhearing your church's praise?
Why might the prospect of God coming to judge be good news for the sea, the fields, and the trees, and for people who have suffered injustice?
What would it mean to sing a “new song” rather than only the familiar ones?
